title: Volunteering for older New Yorkers: programs and stipends
seoTitle: Volunteering for Older Adults in New York
seoDesc: Volunteer roles for older New Yorkers: AmeriCorps Seniors at 55, NYC Aging, HIICAP, county RSVP programs near NJ, state parks, and which roles pay a stipend.
dek: From tutoring kids for a small stipend to counseling neighbors on Medicare, New York has volunteer roles for every schedule. Here is where to sign up in the city, the state and the counties near New Jersey.
keyFacts: AmeriCorps Seniors programs (RSVP, Foster Grandparent, Senior Companion) are open at 55
NYC Foster Grandparents get a $4 an hour tax-free stipend
Rockland RSVP offers optional mileage reimbursement for drivers
NYC HIICAP volunteers serve one day a week, 4 to 6 hours, for at least a year
More than 70 state parks and historic sites have Friends Groups
body:
Older New Yorkers can volunteer through the AmeriCorps Seniors programs starting at 55, through NYC Aging and NYC Service in the five boroughs, and through the county Office for the Aging everywhere else. A few roles pay a small stipend or mileage, such as the $4 an hour tax-free stipend for Foster Grandparents in New York City.

The hardest part is usually picking a starting point. This guide lays out the federal, state, city and county programs, with roles close to New Jersey in Rockland, Westchester and Orange counties. It also covers state park and library volunteering and what health experts say volunteering does for older adults.

What are the AmeriCorps Seniors programs?

AmeriCorps Seniors runs three national volunteer programs, and all three are open to people 55 and older. Local groups host them, so the schedule, stipend and duties depend on the program near you.

ProgramWhat volunteers doTimeStipend
RSVPServe with local organizations on causes they chooseA few hours up to 40 hours a weekSome programs pay a modest stipend to qualified low-income volunteers
Foster Grandparent ProgramMentor and tutor children and young people with exceptional needsNYSOFA says 15 to 40 hours a weekSome programs pay a modest stipend to qualified low-income volunteers
Senior Companion ProgramBefriend older neighbors who have trouble with daily tasks such as shopping or paying billsSet by the local programSome programs pay a modest stipend to qualified low-income volunteers

AmeriCorps says most of its senior programs carry accident, personal liability and excess auto liability insurance for volunteers. To find openings, use the AmeriCorps Seniors Pathfinder tool on americorps.gov.

NYSOFA says RSVP runs in New York City, on Long Island and in most upstate counties. Foster Grandparents serve at Head Start programs, hospitals, public schools, day care centers and juvenile detention centers, working with children with special needs from birth to 21. Senior Companions reach out to adults who need extra help to keep living on their own, and AmeriCorps says the program also gives family caregivers a break.

You don't need a special skill to start. Programs such as HIICAP and the Foster Grandparent Program train volunteers before they begin.

How do I volunteer in New York City?

NYC Aging runs a Volunteer Program with NYC Service. Volunteers must be at least 18 and meet each role's own requirements, such as vaccination or a background check. Sign up on the NYC Aging volunteer portal or call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.

Roles listed by NYC Aging include:

  • Friendly Visiting. Volunteers visit homebound older adults at home and build friendships through shared interests.
  • Health Insurance Information, Counseling and Assistance Program (HIICAP). Volunteers answer Medicare questions and help people apply for Extra Help. It takes extensive training, a state exam each year, at least one day a week of four to six hours and at least a one-year commitment. It's not open to insurance marketers.
  • Keep On Track. Volunteers run monthly blood pressure checks at older adult centers using automatic monitors.
  • Stay Well. Volunteers lead hour-long fitness classes at older adult centers for people of all skill, mobility and fitness levels.
  • Alert and Alive, and Partner to Partner. Volunteers lead discussion groups for older adults or have confidential one-on-one talks with people dealing with loneliness or loss.
  • One-time events. Aging Connect also lists single-day shifts at food pantries, resource fairs and conferences, which suit people with changing schedules.

What does the city's Foster Grandparent Program involve?

NYC Aging's Foster Grandparent Program is for city residents 55 and older who meet income rules. Volunteers support children ages 3 to 12 with special needs. You commit to at least 15 hours a week after a 20-hour orientation. Volunteers get $4 an hour, tax-free, for service and training time. As funding allows, meals and travel to and from volunteer sites may be reimbursed. Email fgp@aging.nyc.gov or call Aging Connect.

For other city roles, NYC Service at nycservice.org lists openings you can search by date, location and impact area.

What volunteer roles does New York State run?

NYSOFA runs two statewide programs that train volunteers to help older adults, and its 59 local offices for the aging recruit volunteers too.

  • HIICAP. Volunteers hand out information, help with office work, speak at events and help counsel people on Medicare.
  • Long Term Care Ombudsman Program. Certified volunteer ombudsmen work to improve care and quality of life for people living in nursing homes and other long term care facilities.

NYSOFA's volunteer flyer says to use the volunteer interest form at aging.ny.gov/volunteer for either one. For HIICAP, someone from NYSOFA or the local program follows up. The same flyer says local offices for the aging rely on volunteers of any age to drive people to appointments, deliver meals at home, staff group meal sites, help in the office and make reassurance calls or friendly visits. Find your county office in NYSOFA's local office directory or call NYSOFA at 1-800-342-9871. The state's New Yorkers Volunteer website lists other openings.

What do county offices near New Jersey offer?

Rockland, Westchester and Orange each post their own volunteer programs. Here is what their own pages say.

Rockland County

The Rockland Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP), run by the county Office for the Aging, matches people 55 and older with local agencies. Volunteers drive home-delivered meals and medical trips, guide museum visitors, staff food pantries, help in libraries and thrift shops and counsel people on health insurance or taxes. RSVP volunteers get accident and liability insurance, optional mileage reimbursement if they drive and recognition for years of service. Call 845-364-2112.

The county's Independence Project needs volunteer drivers of any age with a valid license, to take homebound older adults, people with disabilities and veterans to medical visits and pharmacies. The CHORE service uses weekday volunteers who can do minor household repairs. Rockland's Foster Grandparent Program runs through Head Start of Rockland at 845-429-4122. Volunteers 55 and older who meet income rules mentor students with special needs 15 to 40 hours a week. The county says they get a tax-free stipend, monthly training, paid sick and vacation days, meals during service and help getting to the school. See the Rockland County page.

Westchester County

RSVP of Westchester is an AmeriCorps Seniors program hosted by the nonprofit Volunteer New York!, open to Westchester residents 55 and older. You choose anywhere from a few hours to 40 hours a week. Its page lists orientation, training, supplemental insurance while on duty and travel reimbursement. Host sites include hospitals, senior centers, the Hudson River Museum, Westchester Community College and the county Department of Senior Programs and Services, where volunteers help with HIICAP. Call RSVP of Westchester at 914-227-9318. See the Westchester County page.

Orange County

The Orange County Office for the Aging trains HIICAP volunteers for free and pairs them with mentors. It looks for people who can grasp a lot of information, communicate clearly, bring patience and empathy and give a few hours a week. Call 845-615-3715. See the Orange County page.

  1. Pick a cause and a schedule. Decide how many hours a week you can give and if you'd rather work with kids, older adults, food, parks or paperwork.
  2. Call one number. In the city, call Aging Connect. Elsewhere, call your county Office for the Aging or RSVP.
  3. Ask about costs and coverage. Ask whether the role pays a stipend or mileage and whether volunteers are insured.
  4. Expect screening. NYC Aging notes that some roles need a background check or proof of vaccination.
  5. Finish the training. HIICAP and the Foster Grandparent Program both need training before you start.
  6. Log your hours. Rockland RSVP has an online form for entering hours served and recognizes years of service.

Can I volunteer at a state park or a library?

Yes. New York State Parks says more than seventy of its parks and historic sites have active Friends Groups, which run volunteer projects from nature centers to trail cleanups. Follow the Friends Group link on a park's page, or call the park and ask how to help.

  • I Love My Park Day. A yearly spring event, held on Saturday, May 2 in 2026, with beach cleanups, trail restoration and tree and flower plantings at over 100 state parks, historic sites and public lands. It's organized by Parks & Trails New York with State Parks and the Department of Environmental Conservation.
  • Camper Assistance Program. Seasoned campers share their know-how with other people at state campgrounds.

Libraries use volunteers too. Rockland RSVP places volunteers in libraries, and the NIA lists libraries among good places to start. Ask your branch what volunteer help it needs.

What do health experts say about volunteering?

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says being lonely or socially isolated is not good for your overall health. It lists volunteering among the meaningful activities that may help older adults keep their well-being and independence.

The NIA says older adults who stay active are less likely to develop certain diseases, such as some forms of dementia, heart disease and stroke, and that studies suggest older adults who volunteer or stay active say they feel happier and healthier. It suggests volunteering at a school, library, museum, hospital or animal shelter, serving meals, running errands for people with limited mobility and helping at a community garden or park.

If your parent has slowed down since a loss or a move, a set weekly shift can give the week a shape. Start small, with one morning, and add more later. Our senior centers guide lists another easy place to start, and our caregiver support guide covers help for the family member doing the caring.

Where the money isWhat the official page says
NYC Foster Grandparent Program$4 an hour, tax-free; meals and travel may be reimbursed as funding allows
Rockland Foster Grandparent ProgramTax-free stipend, meals during service, paid sick and vacation days
RSVP of WestchesterTravel reimbursement and supplemental insurance while on duty
Rockland RSVPOptional mileage reimbursement for volunteers who drive
AmeriCorps Seniors, in generalSome programs pay a modest stipend to qualified low-income volunteers; most carry insurance

If your parent gets SNAP, Medicaid or other benefits, ask the program how its stipend is treated before signing up.

faq.q: How can my mom find volunteer work in Rockland County?
faq.a: If she is 55 or older, call the Rockland Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP) at the county Office for the Aging, 845-364-2112. It matches volunteers with local agencies for roles like meal delivery, food pantries, library help and museum guiding, with insurance and optional mileage reimbursement for drivers.

faq.q: Where can my dad volunteer with older adults in Manhattan?
faq.a: Call NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 or sign up on the NYC Aging volunteer portal. Roles include Friendly Visiting, Medicare counseling through HIICAP, blood pressure checks and fitness classes at older adult centers, and one-day shifts at food pantries and resource fairs.

faq.q: Do Foster Grandparent volunteers get paid?
faq.a: They get a small stipend. In New York City, NYC Aging pays Foster Grandparents $4 an hour, tax-free, for service and training time. Volunteers must be 55 or older, meet income rules and give at least 15 hours a week.

faq.q: Can I volunteer to help people with Medicare questions?
faq.a: Yes. The Health Insurance Information, Counseling and Assistance Program (HIICAP) trains volunteers across New York. Use the interest form at aging.ny.gov/volunteer, or call your county office. In Orange County, call 845-615-3715. Insurance marketers can't serve as HIICAP counselors in New York City.

faq.q: How old do you have to be for AmeriCorps Seniors?
faq.a: You must be 55 or older for RSVP, the Foster Grandparent Program and the Senior Companion Program. Use the AmeriCorps Seniors Pathfinder tool on americorps.gov to find openings near you.

faq.q: Can I volunteer in a New York state park?
faq.a: Yes. More than seventy state parks and historic sites have Friends Groups that run volunteer projects. You can also join I Love My Park Day each spring (it was May 2 in 2026), or call your local park and ask how to help.
